name: West Face - West Rib (Lichtenhorn / West Peak)
approach: From the Old Lake Valhalla/Lake Janus Trailhead on Smith Brook Road (~4,150 ft), follow the trail toward Union Gap and continue to Lichtenberg Pass, then leave the trail to approach the base of the west face.
descent: Descend via the northeast slope of the peak back toward the approach trail.

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. Campfires are prohibited at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

bivy.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
bivy.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
bivy.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
bivy.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

itinerary: Single day, car to car. Drive from Seattle (roughly 2 to 2.5 hours to the Smithbrook Trailhead via US 2) or from Leavenworth (about 45 minutes), start early, reach the PCT saddle above Lake Valhalla in about 2 hours, climb the west face and rib in 1 to 1.5 hours, and descend the Northeast Slope past Lichtenwasser Lake to the road in around 2.5 hours — roughly 6 to 7 hours total. If you would rather make it an overnight, camp at Lake Valhalla (dispersed sites, set well back from the shore, campfires prohibited) and climb the face the following morning with a light pack; this also positions you for The Lichtenhorn in good early light, which is when the west face is in the sun.

waypoints.name: Lichtenberg Boulders (granitic boulder field off the Valhalla trail)
Lake Valhalla (below the west face; camping, no campfires)
Lichtenberg Mountain main summit (5,844 ft; the route tops out on the west peak at ~5,800 ft)

name: Northeast Face
approach: From the Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead (the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where the road is gated), follow Dutch Miller Gap Trail 1030 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley about 14-15 miles to Dutch Miller Gap, passing Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the Williams Lake trail junction along the way. Little Big Chief sits immediately southwest of the gap, reached from the gap itself by an off-trail scramble up the peak's east slope/northeast ridge, with a short but exposed class 4 notch as the crux below the summit. An alternate, longer approach comes from the east via the Necklace Valley Trail off Foss River Road (Skykomish/US 2 side), crossing La Bohn Gap before dropping to Dutch Miller Gap. A second long approach comes from the southeast: the Waptus River Trail from Salmon La Sac to Waptus Lake (with an unbridged river ford below the lake), a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, then the Dutch Miller Gap trail up past Lake Ivanhoe to the gap. For this specific route: continue the standard Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail all the way up to Dutch Miller Gap, then climb directly above the gap onto the peak's northeast ridge/face — no cross-country detour into Summit Chief Valley needed.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or rappel the short roped pitches into the east-face cirque, then descend the snowfield and the heather and rock steps of the northeast ridge toward Dutch Miller Gap — or, via the alternate approach, back into the northeast basin.

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
bivy.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for Iron Cap Mountain's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
bivy.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is gated at Dingford Creek, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. Burnt Boot Peak is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
bivy.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to Little Big Chief Mountain, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the Dutch Miller Gap trail climbs past Lake Ivanhoe to the gap, where the northeast face scramble starts. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is not a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
bivy.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
bivy.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

itinerary: Usually a 2-3 day trip and often combined with a neighbouring peak (Summit Chief or Overcoat) from a backcountry camp near Dutch Miller Gap or Summit Chief Lake: approach and camp on day 1, climb the northeast ridge/face and return to camp on day 2, hike out on day 3. Strong parties climb it as a long day from a camp already at the gap.

name: North Face
approach: Same range approach as the standard line: Elbow Lake Trailhead, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack (unofficial log crossing ~1/4 mile downstream of the marked ford), off-trail to Green Creek, cross Green Creek, ascend a rock buttress near 3,800 ft, then travel the Green Creek Glacier to the base of the North Face.
descent: Rappel the looker's right side of the face on scattered pin/tat anchors, or downclimb the Southeast Ridge instead.

bivy.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
bivy.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
bivy.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
bivy.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
bivy.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

itinerary: Best done from a camp in the upper Green Creek basin. Day 1: drive in (allow extra time if FR 38 is gated or washed out at MP 7), cross the Middle Fork on the log, hike the Elbow Lake Trail and the Green Creek climbers' path, and camp below the Green Creek Glacier. Day 2: early start onto the glacier, climb steep snow to the base, cross the moat, climb the four pitches of the North Face, then descend either by rappelling the lookers-right side or by downclimbing the Southeast Ridge; break camp and walk out. Strong parties go car-to-car in a long day. The most efficient use of the approach is to combine routes — North Face up and Southeast Ridge down, or vice versa — or to take in Cinderella Peak across the col. The full Green Creek Circuit that includes this summit is 5.6, Grade IV, about 25 pitches over 13 miles with roughly 7,000 ft of gain, taking 10-14 hours for the traverse portion.

name: South Couloir
approach: From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road), the Elbow Lake Trail reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack River within a few minutes. The bridge is gone and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible during high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently in place. One group used a log crossing roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction; another used an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it, and treat the crossing as the crux of the day in terms of consequence. Once across, follow the Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old-growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback (near Hildebrand Creek), find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off and heading up the Green Creek drainage. It is marked with small blue diamond trail markers. Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, then up through the brush-filled Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. The Green Glacier approach is 5 miles one way with 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead over trail, climbers' trail, boulder fields, scree and slabs. For the South Couloir specifically, continue up the basin and climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of Little Sister, then traverse onto the south side and up into the gully. In deep winter one party found hard snow all the way to the col; snowshoes were left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
descent: Reverse the line: downclimb and rappel the gully, then descend south-side snow back to the col and reverse the Green Creek approach.
itinerary: A long single day from the Elbow Lake Trailhead: a winter party left about 7 a.m., reached the summit around 1 p.m. and was back after dark, about 12 hours and roughly 10 miles and 5,000 ft car to car. The line has also been skied as part of a multi-day traverse of the whole range.

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trailhead (FR 38, Middle Fork Nooksack)

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: Elbow Lake Trailhead, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack (unofficial log crossing recommended), off-trail through brush to Green Creek, cross Green Creek, ascend the rock buttress near 3,800 ft, then travel the Green Creek Glacier — staying on the lookers-left (south) side — up to the Cinderella-Little Sister col to start the ridge.
descent: Downclimb the route, or rappel the North Face on scattered tat and pin anchors.
itinerary: Best as an overnight. Day 1: drive to the Elbow Lake Trailhead (allow extra time if FR 38 is gated or washed out at MP 7), cross the Middle Fork on the log, hike the Elbow Lake Trail and Green Creek climbers' path, and camp in the upper Green Creek basin below the glacier. Day 2: early start onto the Green Creek Glacier, cross the moat at the Cinderella-Little Sister col, climb the three pitches of the Southeast Ridge and the fourth-class finish to the summit, then either downclimb the ridge or rappel the North Face to the glacier, break camp and walk out. Fit parties do it car-to-car in a long day; combining it with the North Face (up one, down the other) or continuing to Cinderella Peak makes far better use of the approach. The full Green Creek Circuit, which takes in this ridge, is Grade IV 5.6, roughly 25 pitches and 13 miles with about 7,000 ft of gain, and takes 10-14 hours for the traverse alone.

name: West Face
approach: Best reached via the Green Creek Circuit: Elbow Lake Trailhead, cross the Middle Fork Nooksack, off-trail to Green Creek and the Green Creek Glacier, then around to the west side of Little Sister (often linked with Skookum Peak on the circuit).
descent: Reverse the west-most rib to a second, lower notch, where snow or a rappel leads back down to the glacier.
