name: Standard Scramble (Jefferson Creek / Hamma Hamma approach)
approach: From Hoodsport, drive about 14 miles north on US 101 to Hamma Hamma River Road (FR 25); follow it roughly 6.5 miles to FR 2480, then FR 2480 about 3 miles to FR 2401, then FR 2401 roughly 7–7.5 miles to the Jefferson Creek crossing / Jefferson Lake Trailhead area (~2,440 ft). A faint boot path on the north side of the creek leads through forest and brush into the basins below Pershing's east side, then up gullies to the summit ridge. Confirm current road status with Olympic National Forest before driving — FR 2480/2401 have a history of washouts and occasional fire closures. From the boot path, the route rises via a rocky gully to a small basin around 4,300 ft, then continues into a basin east of the summit near 5,400 ft before the final snow/rock gully to the ridge.
descent: Reverse the route: down-climb the ridge crest and the short Class 4 step, then descend the snow/rock gully and basins back to the Jefferson Creek trail and trailhead.

bivy.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
bivy.notes: This is the staging spot for Mount Pershing and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
bivy.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
bivy.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

itinerary: Long day trip (~8 miles round trip, 10–11 hours) from the Jefferson Creek trailhead off FR 2401 in the Hamma Hamma drainage; a basin camp is an option for a more relaxed overnight pace.

name: West Ridge
approach: From US Highway 2 near Index, turn onto Forest Road 62 (also called No Name Creek Road / Proctor Creek Road / Cavanaugh Lake Road). Follow FR-62 about 3.4-3.5 miles to the first junction (~1,600-1,650 ft) and bear left. Continue about 1 mile to a second junction (~2,380 ft) and bear left again. Drive roughly another 0.7-1 mile of increasingly rough road to its end (~2,800 ft), where there is a small pullout/parking area. An unmarked, steep, well-trodden gully directly opposite the pullout marks the boot-path trailhead. Note: FR-62 crosses private industrial timberland and its gate at the highway is frequently locked at the owner's discretion — some parties have had to walk or e-bike an additional ~5+ miles and ~2,500 ft of road to reach this trailhead.
descent: Descend the same West Ridge boot path back to the FR-62 trailhead.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

itinerary: Single-day, car-to-car outing: drive FR-62 to the road-end trailhead (allow extra time/mileage if the highway gate is locked), climb the West Ridge boot path to the summit (roughly 2-3 hours of climbing), enjoy summit views, then descend the same way. Total car-to-car time is commonly reported as 4.5+ hours given the steepness and route-finding, longer in winter conditions or if the road gate forces an extended approach.

name: East Ridge (Iodine Gulch – Bathtub Lakes)
approach: From the Verlot Public Service Center on the Mountain Loop Highway, continue east about 4.6 miles and turn right onto Forest Road 4020 (Schweitzer Creek Road, signed for Boardman Lake/Ashland Lakes/Bear-Pinnacle Lake). Follow FR 4020 for 2.7 miles to a junction, take the right fork onto FR 4021, and continue 1.4 miles on a rough road to the Pinnacle Lake Trailhead (about 2,700 ft; small ~15-car lot, no toilet). Hike the Pinnacle Lake Trail to the lake, walk around its southwest shore to Iodine Creek, and follow the creek up through Iodine Gulch to its top; turn right and continue a short distance to the Bathtub Lakes basin. From there, continue scrambling west to reach Mount Pilchuck's summit. In October the road to Pinnacle Lake trailhead is rough enough that high clearance is advisable; in a high-water year the lake trail itself can wash out.
descent: Reverse the route back through Bathtub Lakes and Iodine Gulch to Pinnacle Lake and the trailhead.

bivy.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
bivy.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
bivy.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a state conservation area rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the federal pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed

itinerary: Single day: drive to the Pinnacle Lake Trailhead, hike to Pinnacle Lake, scramble via Iodine Gulch to Bathtub Lakes (optional turnaround point), then continue to the summit and return the same way — a longer, more committing full-day outing than the standard trail.

name: Mount Pilchuck Trail (Standard Route)
approach: From Granite Falls, follow WA-92 east and then the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 10-11 miles to the Verlot Public Service Center. Continue about 1 mile past Verlot, cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River, and turn right (south) onto Mount Pilchuck Road (FR 42). Follow FR 42 for about 6.8 miles — rough, washboarded gravel for the first ~4.7 miles and paved for the last ~1.9, with the gravel's condition varying by year — to the Mount Pilchuck Trailhead parking area (roughly 3,000-3,100 ft). In years when FR 42 is gated below the trailhead (common in shoulder season), the hike instead starts from the Heather Lake Trailhead, adding roughly 5 miles and substantial elevation gain each way.
descent: Descend the same Mount Pilchuck Trail back to the FR 42 trailhead; there is no separate descent route.
itinerary: Single-day round trip: drive to the FR 42 trailhead, hike up via Trail #700, spend time at the lookout, then descend the same trail — a full day out once drive time from the Seattle/Everett area is included.

name: Hester Lake Route
approach: Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) to the Dingford Creek Trailhead (~1,400 ft). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail, crossing several creeks, toward the Hester Lake basin (roughly 5-6 miles) before leaving the trail to begin the off-trail scramble.
descent: Descend the same general line back through the boulder field and Hester Lake basin to the Dingford Creek Trail; several parties report their descent line diverging from the ascent for lack of a fixed route.

bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
bivy.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is cut by a washout at milepost 17.3 that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft; the Forest Service's road-damage alert of June 30, 2026 lists it with no reopening date. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

itinerary: Full, often long day: Dingford Creek TH -> ~5-6 mi trail to the Hester Lake basin -> off-trail gully/boulder-field/ridge scramble to the summit -> reverse descent. At least one trip report logged roughly 10.5 hours car-to-car; start early and carry a headlamp.
